doc.title: Sam Kininger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 27, 2011

title: Writing music and band members' training
summary: Combining funk with more complex changes; group composing; band members' backgrounds.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well wouldn’t it be interesting to be able to take the funk feel that you usually work in, and try to combine it with more complex chord changes or something like that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

Yes. I mean I try to do that when I write too as well, like for my stuff. I just do not make it a one chord thing, you know, where there’s a bridge and there’s a C section at the end, and then go back to somewhere else. Make it a little bit more interesting I guess, for the listener and for the musician.

A lot of it is us together in a group situation, where I’ll have an idea for the melody and it’s definitely a group. The past two situations have been. I haven’t really come in with charts you know. But I’ll have an idea of a tune and the way it’s supposed to go. And this is another important thing about the whole situation is having people get it. You know, like having people who understand what you’re talking about. Sometimes it can be a different language. Some people are like, “What do you mean?” And you’re like uh. So it’s good to have a chemistry with the people that you play with over the years, that sort of get what you’re saying, you know, and you don’t have to be super technical about it.
Are most of the people in your band, are they — I hate to use the word — but are they college-trained musicians and schooled?

Some. Just, well actually one. Amy, the keyboard player. She went to a classical school in North Carolina. Both Aaron and Nikki both went to Berklee but Aaron is self-taught as a bass player, and Nicky grew up like in churches so she was like — I say myself and Amy are the only really classically trained in the band.
